_read_me: The rules both checks run on. Two kinds, kept apart on purpose.
1. tokenHashes - the names that must never appear here or in the published
tarball. They are stored as SALTED HASHES, never as text.
THE HASHES DO NOT HIDE ANYTHING. Say that here, at the top, because the
sentences that follow describe what changed and could be read as saying
the opposite. A hash of a short name confirms a guess; it does not keep
a secret, and the audit recorded further down this file recovered every
entry on the current list from a wordlist. Nothing may be put on this
list on the strength of the hashing - see _tokenHashes for the two
rules that govern what may go on it.
The previous version of this file listed them in the clear, captioned
with what each one was, in a PUBLIC repository, and it was also the one
file the sweep skipped, so the sweep structurally could not see it.
Nothing is skipped now. What that change removed was the PUBLICATION -
the list, the captions, and the shape of the platform, handed to a
stranger who had not asked. It did not make any of these names secret,
and it was never capable of doing so.
2. patterns - generic shapes that give nothing away (SQL keywords, a source
map marker, a run of nineteen digits). Their `regex` is base64 so that
this file is not a match for itself; that is a self-reference fix, NOT
secrecy, and they decode to exactly what their label says.
`npm run rules:show` prints the decoded patterns and the hash count.
What the hashes do NOT do, measured rather than estimated: they are a
confirmation oracle, and the recovery rate is known. A wordlist built from
the platform's own tracked files recovers ALL of them - 8 of 8, every entry
on the current list - and a wordlist of ordinary English and technical
vocabulary recovers none of them, 0 of 8 over 236,132 candidates. An
earlier version of this paragraph said 'most of them', which understated
the very property this page depends on; the real figure is all of them,
and it is the one to plan against.
That is accepted, not overlooked. Nothing on this list has access value,
nothing on it can be rotated, and confirming any of it buys a reader
nothing they could act on - which is a property of what is on the list,
so it is the list's contents that have to be policed, and _tokenHashes
states the two rules that do it. The gain was never the strings; it was
losing the captions that said what each name was, and losing the exemption
that stopped the sweep from reading the one file that mattered.
Keeping this file in the public repository is also a decision: behind a
secret, neither check could run for an outside contributor or in a fork, so
it would report success in exactly the case it exists for.
_tokenLength: The SCANNER'S BOUNDS, in characters: the shortest and longest candidate it
will hash. They are not a description of the entries, and they are not to be
adjusted to fit the entries. Every entry has to lie inside them; that is a
constraint on what may be added, not a measurement to be kept up to date.
DO NOT TIDY THESE NUMBERS INWARDS to match whatever is on the list today.
Two things go wrong in the one edit, and both look like housekeeping. The
decoders size themselves from the lower bound, so raising it stops every
encoded form shorter than the new floor from being looked at - silently, with
the checks still green. And the pair is published, so narrowing it sharpens a
public range at the same moment. A name that falls outside the bounds means
WIDEN them; it never means trim the bounds, and it never means leave the name
uncovered.
The lower bound earns its care twice: a threshold chosen without reference to
what is being looked for is how a check comes to report success about what it
never read. The first version demanded 18 bytes of plaintext before it would
look at base64, and nothing on the list was that long.
A range is a disclosure, so it is not made wider than the scanner needs: the
one class whose space a length hint collapses is not on this list any more
(see _numbers). What remains is long enough that a length bound adds nothing a
wordlist did not already give, which is the limitation _read_me concedes.
blindSpots() derives its statement from these numbers, so it cannot claim a
coverage the thresholds do not give.
_tokenHashes: sha256(`${salt}:${token.toLowerCase()}`). A finding reports the hash prefix
and the file and line - never the token, because a CI log on a public
repository is as public as this file.
An entry is matched only in its letters/digits/underscore spelling: every
candidate the scanner builds is drawn from [a-z0-9_], so an entry that
itself contains any other character can never match anything. That cannot
be checked from here, because this file holds hashes, so it is stated in
blindSpots() and printed on every run instead of being assumed.
THE HASHING HIDES NOTHING. It is a lint aid: it keeps the list out of the
clear so that this file is not itself the publication, and it confirms a
guess for anyone who already has one. The measured recovery rate is in
_read_me. Everything below follows from that.
TWO RULES GOVERN WHAT MAY GO ON THIS LIST. They are different rules and
they fail in opposite directions, so both are stated.
RULE 1 - what may not go on it because it would be UNSATISFIABLE.
An entry must not be a substring of text this repository legitimately
prints. Such an entry can never be satisfied: the only ways out are
deleting it or narrowing the scanner, and narrowing the scanner is
strictly worse. There is no mechanical test for it, because this file
holds hashes and not names. The sweep going red IS the test.
RULE 2 - what may not go on it because it would be EFFECTIVE.
Anything whose harm IS the confirmation of a guess must never be added, in
any spelling: a credential, an API key or token, a password, a session,
subscription or contract identifier, a certificate serial, a hostname that
grants access, personal data. The discriminator is not sensitivity in the
abstract. A table name confirmed is a fact about a schema a stranger
cannot reach; an identifier confirmed IS the identifier. This list is
public and it answers questions, so putting one of those on it would be
publishing it with extra steps. Nothing on the list today is from that
class, and that was checked rather than assumed. Something from that class
does not belong in this repository at all - the answer is to remove it and
rotate it, never to add a hash of it here.
HOW TO SPELL AN ENTRY. Store a name of several segments GLUED, with no
separator: 'alphabeta', not 'alpha_beta' - an example whose two spellings
are both inside the length range this file declares, so it can be tried as
written. The
scanner cuts at every separator
and at every case boundary and then offers each window BOTH glued and
underscore-joined, so the glued spelling is produced by every separated
spelling as well as by a boundary-free run - while the underscore spelling
cannot be produced from a run that has no boundary in it at all, which is
how a name appears in a minified bundle or in decoded hex. Measured over
ten placements: glued 10 of 10, underscore-joined 9 of 10, and there is no
placement where the separated form wins.
CHANGES TO THE LIST are recorded here, because changing a rule that has
just started failing is exactly the move that must never pass unexplained.
What a later maintainer needs is the rule that was applied, the lengths,
and any narrowing. What an entry MEANS is a caption, and captions are what
this file exists to have stopped writing.
- One entry of 8 characters REMOVED under rule 1. It had been on the list
since the first commit, and a file in this repository had been breaking
it since the first commit; only a gap in the scanner kept that green.
The normal answer to a finding is to change the file, and that file
could not change.
- One entry REPLACED under rule 1, 7 characters out and 10 in. The
7-character form was unsatisfiable; the longer form is not. Declared
narrowing: one spelling that the old entry matched is no longer matched,
and it is the spelling that made the old entry unsatisfiable - on its
own it identifies nothing.
- That replacement was first stored underscore-joined and is now stored
glued, under the spelling rule above: one more placement covered, no
other change.
- The remaining six were audited against both rules in the same round and
stay.
A NOTE ON THIS NOTE. Earlier wordings of these entries described what the
changed entries were ABOUT, and taken together those descriptions narrowed
the candidate space for a live entry further than the hash alone does -
the same caption failure _numbers refuses for numbers on the facing page.
The wording is corrected here going forward and nothing more is claimed:
the earlier text is in this repository's history and in the pull request
that carried it, and editing a published file does not unpublish it, which
is the same reasoning CONTRIBUTING.md gives for not squash-merging. The
rule that follows applies from now on - record the rule, the lengths and
the narrowing, never the subject.

licence, github.com is this repository, viafrei.de and mcp.viafrei.de are
the public service. The loopback and the reserved .invalid TLD belong to
the offline tests; the npm registry appears in the publish workflow and in
_samples: Each tarball/embedded-source pattern carries a `sample`: a base64 string
that the pattern must match. The gate's self-test poisons a copy of the
real tarball with it, so a rule added here is a case added there and the
self-test never has to spell a forbidden string out itself. The repository
patterns carry no sample - one of them is a run of nineteen digits, and a
sample of that is the very thing this repository may not contain.
_numbers: Numbers are NOT hashed, and this is the round-3 defect being repaired.
A hash of a value drawn from a small enumerable space is not a hash, it is
the value with extra steps: a reviewer exhausted the space of one such class
in 49 milliseconds on a laptop, with the salt taken from this file and no
wordlist at all. Publishing a minimum length made it worse.
So that class is not on the hash list any more. It is covered instead by the
opposite construction: an ALLOW-list of the numbers this repository may
contain, with no captions. An allow-list gives a reader nothing - these are
the numbers that are here, which they can already see - and it is strictly
stronger than the hashes were, because it catches every internal value of
this shape, including the ones nobody thought to add.
That sentence has to be TRUE OF EVERY ENTRY, and in round 4 it was not. One
entry was in no tracked file: it was here only to silence a finding about a
value the same commit had taken OUT of the tree, so diffing this list
against the working tree isolated it in one step - and an entry a reader can
isolate is a caption pointing at the value, which is the whole thing the
inverse construction exists to avoid. It is gone. The occurrences it was
covering are in the history, they cannot be taken back, and they are
recorded as residue below instead - by content address, which says nothing
the sweep does not print for itself.
So the invariant, checkable rather than promised: every entry here occurs in
the working tree. `git grep` each one; if one does not, it is a caption and
it comes out.
The window and this list have to describe the same class, and thresholds()
refuses when they stop doing so. Setting the window to 20-25 digits used to
make the rule inert while both legs still printed PASS.
Adding one: if a number in this range is genuinely part of this repository,
put it here. If it is an internal value, it does not belong in the file at
all, and the point of the check is that you have to make that choice.
_historyNumberResidue: What could not be undone.
These blobs are in this repository's history and hold a bare number in the
numbers window that is not on the allow-list. They are pushed, so they are
fetched; a rewrite does not unpublish an object a stranger already has, and
GitHub keeps an unreferenced blob reachable by its sha. Residue, recorded -
not a repair.
Each entry names a BLOB by content address and the number of findings that
blob yields. It is not a value, not a path and not a commit, and it cannot
be widened: a blob is immutable, so an exemption for one can never come to
cover a line somebody adds later. It suppresses the `number` rule ONLY, in
the history leg ONLY; a private name or a pattern in the same blob still
fails, and the working tree is never exempt from anything.
Why this is not the caption the allow-list entry was: without these entries
the sweep PRINTS these same locations - file, line and commit - in red, on
every run, into a public CI log, because that is what a finding does. Naming
them here costs nothing that is not already the tool's required output. The
allow-list entry cost the value, which the sweep never prints at all. That
asymmetry is the whole of the trade.
What check-leaks does about an entry that has stopped being true, stated
here because this is the document a reader is sent to for the contract:
- An entry that matches NO blob in the history is a FINDING (exit 1).
- A blob that yields a different number of findings than is claimed here
is a FINDING (exit 1) too. A blob cannot change, so if these disagree,
the scanner changed - which is the thing worth being told about.
- An entry whose `findings` is not a whole number of at least 1 is a
REFUSAL (exit 2), and that one is different on purpose: the other two
are read AFTER every blob has been read, whereas a claim that is not a
number cannot be checked against anything at all. An unverifiable claim
that still suppresses is a check that has not checked.
The first two used to be refusals, and used to be justified here as the
silent-skip class. That was wrong twice over. A run that reaches them has
read every blob in the history, so 'I could not look' is false; and a
suppression that stops applying makes the run LOUDER, not quieter, because
everything it used to hide is reported. Wrong, but wrong in the safe
direction - nothing was ever hidden by the mistake.
_patterns: Each pattern is stored base64-encoded AND reversed, and both halves of that
are load-bearing. base64 keeps the file from matching its own rules when it
is read as text; reversing keeps it from matching them when it is read as
base64, which the scanner now also does. Neither is secrecy - the shapes are
generic and `npm run rules:show` prints them - it is a file that must not be
a hit for itself while still being scanned like every other file.
